title: Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life
note: Facts verified in the full text (archive.org djvu text). Credit line: Nir Eyal with Julie Li; stories name Nir Eyal as author.

facts.claim: Eyal and his daughter (their only child) were doing an activity book for dads and daughters: name each other's favorite things, build a paper airplane from a page, then answer 'If you could have any superpower, what would it be?' He was on his phone, said 'Just a second. I just need to respond to this one thing.' She went quiet; when he looked up she was gone. He says the same scene had played out countless times.

After apologizing he tried a digital detox: a flip phone (gave up: no GPS, saved addresses, audiobooks), a print newspaper subscription (stack of unread papers while he watched TV news), a 1990s word processor without internet (he flipped through unrelated books on the shelf). 'I'd just replaced one distraction with another.'
First step: recognize that distraction starts from within. 'Time management is pain management'; distraction is an attempt to escape discomfort.

Four steps to reimagine an internal trigger (from Jonathan Bricker): look for the discomfort preceding the distraction; write down the trigger (time, activity, feeling) on a Distraction Tracker; explore the sensation with curiosity; beware liminal moments. Eyal's own urge: googling something while writing, which he calls a diversion from difficult work.
Ten-minute rule: when Eyal wants to check his phone he tells himself it is fine to give in, but not now; wait ten minutes, 'surfing the urge'. After ten minutes the urge has usually passed.

To-do lists: tasks get pushed day after day; start from values instead. 'You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it's distracting you from.' Timeboxing = deciding what you will do and when; goal is a calendar with no white space; success is whether you did what you planned. Three life domains: you, relationships, work.

Eyal and his wife Julie bickered about undone housework; he admits he did less than his share and did not see her tasks; evenings ended in late dinners, hurt feelings and sometimes tears. On one of their date days they listed every household task each did; her list was much longer. They split the jobs and timeboxed them on their schedules.
Eyal schedules weekly time with his daughter: they wrote over a hundred activities on paper strips in a 'fun jar' and pull one every Friday afternoon. He and Julie schedule a date twice a month.

Precommitment / Ulysses pact. Effort pact: kSafe (formerly Kitchen Safe), a container with a timer lock by David Krippendorf and Ryan Tseng; apps SelfControl, Freedom, Forest (a virtual tree dies if you leave the app).

Price pact: NEJM smoking study cited (control 6%, $800 reward group 17%, $150 deposit group 52% among those who accepted). Eyal's own: the gym was free in his apartment complex but he kept skipping. He taped a crisp hundred-dollar bill to the wall calendar next to the date of his next workout and bought a ninety-nine-cent lighter: burn the calories or burn the bill ('burn or burn'). He says he has used it over three years, gained twelve pounds of muscle and never burned the bill.
Eyal says precommitments should be used only after the other steps (internal triggers, traction time, external triggers).
Eyal reports that ego depletion (willpower as a limited resource) is disputed; Dweck's study found depletion only in those who believed willpower is limited.

rejected.claim: Quote 'Distraction doesn't come from outside. It comes from inside. We're escaping discomfort.' as verbatim.
rejected.reason: Paraphrase; book's line is 'distraction starts from within'.

rejected.claim: 'A to-do list is the enemy of attention control' and 'If you do something else in that slot you are deceiving yourself' as quotes.
Order: timebox you first, then relationships, then work.
rejected.reason: Book names three domains and starts with 'you' time, but the strict sleep/exercise/eat order is not supported as stated.

rejected.claim: Removing apps from home screen cuts impulsive opens by 40 percent.
Willpower is limited and every decision depletes it.
